chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
title: Following Tatum's runs and his key-change tricks
summary: Stewart explains how he followed Tatum's fast runs and sudden modulations through an open ear, and says he grew more with Tatum than anyone.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: How did you -- one of the things I wanted -- like when you're playing very, very fast and, like say, when you're playing at that speed and somebody modulates,

how do you -- I mean like one of the things you were playing real fast, you know, the chorus gives you a chance to kind of -- you can breathe a little bit easier because you know where the tune is going.

But now, if you're playing at that kind of a speed and the guy modulates it, how do you -- I mean, do you know immediately -- I mean, do you know immediately that he's modulated it? Did it take you -- you know, because I like, for instance, when mean sometimes when (inaudible) Tatum was playing those incredible runs, they're so fast --

-- that I'm trying to figure out how you were able to pick the notes to play because it's almost impossible sometimes when you hear him play to even know what notes he played because they go by so swiftly.

That's right. Well, I imagine that is -- the good part about that is that I had that good ear, and I always used to say I kept my ears open, you know, and fortunately, I was able to keep up with what was happening with Tatum.
Did you feel as though you grew, that you grew more playing with him than with other guys that you played before?
Yes. I grew more with him than anyone
By listening to what he was doing and the tricks that he played also.
Well, like what kind of tricks do you mean?

Well, like when you say modulation into those, some of those strange keys when we hadn't rehearsed in those keys. He would invariably do those little tricks at times, you know, on the jobs that we played. Without any warning he would play the first part, a solo in a regular key and immediately go into another key. And if you don't keep your ears open, if you didn't have your ears open, there wasn't any way you could go along with it.
You were left in the lurch.
You were left in the lurch. That's for sure.
I was very thankful, you know. That was one of my greatest experiences in this business.
